explanations.explanation: That's the word, baker. The LORD tells Moses the oil is "to keep the lamps burning continually" (Leviticus 24:2). No off switch, no break. I once spent years in the dark, so a light that never goes out sounds like a dream to me.

Seven days sounds like a nice, tidy number, but it's not what the LORD says. He asks for oil "to keep the lamps burning continually" (Leviticus 24:2). That means the light keeps going with no end date on it. A week is a good run for a candle, but this is bigger.

Feasts are on the mind after the last few passages, so I get it. But the LORD doesn't tie the light to a feast. He says the lamps are kept burning "continually" (Leviticus 24:2). That's the whole time, not just the party days.
Evening it is. Aaron tends the lamps "from evening until morning" (Leviticus 24:3). So his shift starts when the sun goes down. That's the night shift, baker, and I respect any man who works it.

Midnight is a real hour, but it's not where the shift starts. The text says Aaron tends the lamps "from evening until morning" (Leviticus 24:3). So he's on the job well before the middle of the night. If he started at midnight, the lamps would have a long dark gap, and I know all about dark gaps.

Noon would be a strange time to start a lamp job, baker. The sun is at its highest, and nobody needs help seeing. The text says Aaron tends the lamps "from evening until morning" (Leviticus 24:3). That's when the light is actually needed.

True. The LORD calls it "a permanent statute for the generations to come" (Leviticus 24:3). That means this job isn't just for Aaron's one season. It's meant to carry on down the line. Some of my stamps wore out in a few years, so "permanent" is a big word to me.

This one is actually true. The text says, "This is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come" (Leviticus 24:3). So it isn't a short-term gig that wraps up after a season. It's meant to last for the generations. Easy one to second-guess, so no worries.

explanations.answer: On the gold table before the LORD
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The loaves are set "on the table of pure gold before the LORD" (Leviticus 24:6). A gold table for bread. I've never had a counter that nice, and I've baked on a few. Mine had a wobbly leg and a mystery stain.

explanations.answer: On the bronze altar of burnt offering
explanations.explanation: That altar is a real piece of the Tent's setup, but it's not where these loaves go. The LORD says to set them "on the table of pure gold before the LORD" (Leviticus 24:6). Bread on the gold table, not on the altar. Keep the loaves away from anything that burns, baker, I learned that the hard way.

explanations.answer: Inside the ark of the Testimony
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd tuck bread somewhere special, but the ark isn't the spot. The text says the loaves are set "on the table of pure gold before the LORD" (Leviticus 24:6). They're out on a table, in two rows, in plain view. No hiding the bread.
That's the one. "Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD" (Leviticus 24:8). So it's a weekly routine, and it comes with the day of rest. Weekly baking, I love a good schedule.

Once a year would be a very relaxed baking calendar, baker, and I'd sign up. But the text says "Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD" (Leviticus 24:8). That's every week, not every year. Fifty-some batches, and the ovens never get cold.

The new moon is a real marker of time in the Bible, but it's not the one here. The text says "Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD" (Leviticus 24:8). That puts it on the weekly rhythm, not the monthly one.

Israelites, you got it. The bread is set out "on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant" (Leviticus 24:8). So the bread stands there for them, week after week. And the word "permanent" shows up again, so that's twice in one passage.

Good guess if you're thinking big, but the text is narrower here. The bread is set out "on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant" (Leviticus 24:8). The passage names the Israelites, so that's who it's for in these verses.

The text doesn't say foreigners here. It says the bread is set out "on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant" (Leviticus 24:8). Israelites are the ones named. I'm not going to add anything the text doesn't say, baker.

Yes, baker. The bread "belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place" (Leviticus 24:9). So it's their portion. Aaron's family gets to eat the bread from the gold table. I'd say that's a pretty great perk.

That would be a big crowd, but the text points to a smaller group. The bread "belongs to Aaron and his sons" (Leviticus 24:9). They're the ones who eat it, and they do it in a holy place. It's not a community potluck.

Generous idea, but that's not what this verse says. The bread "belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place" (Leviticus 24:9). They are the ones who get it. I'll stick with what the text gives us.

Close, but this one is false. The text says Aaron and his sons "are to eat it in a holy place" (Leviticus 24:9). So it's not a take-it-home, eat-it-in-the-tent kind of bread. Even the best snack has a spot where it's supposed to be eaten.

False is right. Aaron and his sons "are to eat it in a holy place" (Leviticus 24:9). So no wandering off with it to the tents. I've been caught sneaking a cookie to the other room, so I know the temptation.
